topic_summaries.Electric Vehicles and Road Transport Pol:
• GB News and The Guardian both cover Andy Burnham's response to potential EV mandate changes, but GB News frames it as a "refusal to rule out U-turn" while The Guardian presents it as Burnham dismissing reports as "speculation"

• The i takes a dual-threat approach — one piece highlights cyber security vulnerabilities in charging infrastructure, another runs a sceptical consumer opinion piece arguing EVs are becoming "more trouble than they're worth"

• Daily Mail frames road usage data collection via EV satnavs as surveillance ("spy under the bonnet"), emphasising government overreach over transport policy detail
topic_summaries.Prince William and Earthshot Prize:
• The Mirror celebrates William's environmental leadership, focusing on his TIME100 Climate recognition and Earthshot's positive impact; BBC emphasises his direct climate advocacy through the wildfire visit to Treherbert
• The Guardian takes a critical angle absent from other outlets, highlighting environmentalist concerns over Earthshot's choice of a venue linked to a major fossil fuel company
topic_summaries.Cop31 Climate Summit:
• The Guardian dominates coverage with multiple framings — from straight news and explainers to satire (First Dog on the Moon cartoon) and opinion — while the BBC focuses narrowly on the Paris Agreement's scientific and historical context
• The Independent emphasises urgency and present-day British climate impacts; The Guardian and Channel 4 News highlight geopolitical tensions, notably US absence under Trump and the Australia-Turkey hosting dispute
• Channel 4 News takes a distinctive angle, framing Trump and Putin as inadvertent drivers of green energy adoption, contrasting with The Guardian and Independent's more conventional crisis-and-action framing
topic_summaries.Polar Vortex Threat:
• Metro leads polar vortex coverage with alarm, emphasising record-breaking cold and snow risk for the UK, citing Met Office warnings about unprecedented Sudden Stratospheric Warming

• The Mirror focuses on a lesser-known, unspecified impact flagged by scientists rather than weather effects, adding a note of scientific novelty

• The Guardian's articles are unrelated to the polar vortex topic, covering beef industry curriculum suppression, US datacenter fossil fuel use, and penguin guano — suggesting limited Guardian engagement with this story
topic_summaries.UK Net Zero and Energy Policy Debate:
• BBC frames net zero as a public support challenge, emphasising energy affordability as the key test of Labour's clean power ambitions; GB News focuses on costs and risks — heat pump bill transfers, gas backup payments, landlord fines — framing green policy as a financial burden on ordinary people
• GB News consistently highlights tensions and failures in the transition (wind power gaps, rising costs, North Sea drilling restrictions), while The i and The Independent take a more solutions-oriented consumer angle (plug-in solar savings, panel grants)
• BBC and GB News both cover the North Sea oil ban but from contrasting positions — BBC reports it factually including SNP opposition, while GB News frames Labour's Energy Bill as an advancing threat to domestic energy security
topic_summaries.UK Air Pollution and Fog Alerts:
• Evening Standard leads on fog-driven air pollution alerts with London-specific data (borough-level mapping, Sadiq Khan's response); GB News covers the same fog event with a broader national framing
• Metro focuses on Bonfire Night fireworks as the pollution trigger; The Sun prioritises the human safety angle via a multi-vehicle fog crash on the A303
• The Independent shifts focus entirely away from the UK, covering Delhi's air pollution — an outlier among outlets anchored to domestic events
topic_summaries.El Niño and Record Temperatures:
• BBC and The Independent frame El Niño as a record-temperature emergency, with 2026 on track to be the hottest year ever; Daily Mail echoes this alarm while also offering a contrarian "good news" angle on fewer cold-weather deaths
• The Guardian focuses on human and ecological impacts — Latin American banana producers, New Mexico rock formations, and UK marine ecosystems — rather than temperature records
• GB News provides no substantive coverage of the topic, with retrieved articles relating to unconnected stories; Evening Standard takes a consumer-focused angle, linking El Niño to UK supermarket food price rises

Greta Thunberg, the Swedish climate activist who inspired global climate protests several years ago, said climate change is “threatening everything” and that “everything and everyone we love is at stake.”
In comments reported by AP, she told reporters in Antalya: “We should act to protect and benefit people rather than constantly sacrificing the global majority, and the very planet we are all living on, for a fortunate few to keep making unimaginable profits and maintaining geopolitical power,” she told reporters.
Cop31 is the first UN climate summit Thunberg has attended since the Cop26 conference in Glasgow, Scotland, in 2021, where she dismissed promises made by global leaders as “blah, blah, blah.”
Since then, fossil fuel emissions have continued to rise – though they flatlined this year – adding even more planet-heating gas to a beleaguered atmosphere. While many big polluters have taken steps to clean up their economies, none are doing so fast enough to keep global heating to the 1.5C Paris climate target.

Greenpeace has unveiled a giant limestone boulder carved into the likeness of Sir David Attenborough, which it plans to throw into the North Sea to deter bottom trawling.
Dubbed the “Attenboulder”, the sculpture was revealed aboard the campaign group’s ship Arctic Sunrise on the River Thames on Tuesday.


View image in fullscreen
The “Attenboulder” on the MY Arctic Sunrise. Photograph: Andrew McConnell/Greenpeace
It will join the boulders Greenpeace placed in the Southern North Sea marine protected area earlier this month, in protest at the lack of restrictions on fishing in most of it. The Marine Management Organisation has threatened legal action unless Greenpeace stops placing boulders.
The unveiling comes as Blue Planet III renews attention on ocean protection.
Will McCallum, Greenpeace UK’s co-executive director, said: “Right off our coasts the government still allows industrial fishing vessels to bulldoze the seabed and all of the incredible marine life it holds.
“These are supposed to be safe havens for wildlife – not killing grounds. The government’s inaction makes a mockery of the term ‘marine protected area’ and is an insult to Attenborough’s urgent work over many years.”

More than 700 groups ranging from trade unions to disability advocates have urged diplomats to prioritise a “just transition” for the people who will be hit hardest by a shift to a clean economy.

Solar panels can reduce your electricity bills for decades, but installing them typically costs several thousand pounds. The good news is that solar panel grants and other government-backed funding schemes could help cover some or all of the upfront cost, depending on your circumstances.
In 2026, eligible households can access free solar panels through schemes such as ECO4 and the Warm Homes: Local Grant. However, funding is generally targeted at lower-income households or properties with poor energy efficiency, and qualifying doesn't automatically mean you'll receive solar panels.
For homeowners who don't qualify for a grant, other financial support is available to reduce or spread the cost of solar panels, including the government's new Warm Homes Loan Scheme, zero per cent VAT on qualifying installations and payments for surplus electricity exported to the grid.

The Labour-led London authority is behind on its target to replace inefficient gas boilers with heat pumps in council-owned properties
Alamy/PA

Hounslow Council is behind on 80 per cent of the measures needed to meet its ambitious 2030 net zero target, raising fresh doubts over whether the west London borough can become carbon neutral within four years.






Council documents show a series of flagship climate projects have stalled or fallen behind schedule, despite the authority declaring a climate emergency seven years ago.




The council, currently led by a minority Labour administration, declared a climate emergency in 2019 and adopted a climate action emergency plan five years later.





But one year on from its “refreshed” action plan, 80% of its policies are off track.




Its ambitious net zero target is 20 years ahead of the UK Government, which is aiming for the country to effectively be carbon neutral by 2050. 




There is a right-wing movement attempting to push back against net zero policies, which critics claim could stunt economic growth and lead to higher bills.








That is despite the UN warning recently, ahead of the major global Cop31 environmental conference taking place in Turkey this week, that the world will overshoot the key climate threshold of 1.5C warming above pre-industrial levels, beyond which extreme weather events is likely to become more intense and frequent.




In west London, the net zero pledge at highest risk of not being delivered is Hounslow Council’s aim to decarbonise the council’s entire operational estate. 


Hounslow House 
LDRS / Google Maps




The authority’s target includes replacing inefficient gas boilers with heat pumps, installing solar panels and installing energy efficacy measures.




However, only one of the council’s 37 buildings has been decarbonised, with this section of the project rated “high risk” because “the funding required to deliver decarbonisation of council operations to achieve net zero by 2030 is significant, and not currently identified or available”.




A further 29 assets have been partially decarbonised, and seven have not been decarbonised at all.




Hounslow has also committed to decarbonising 16,000 council-managed social homes by 2030. 




Progress on the move stalled this year, with only 150 homes fully decarbonised, and no further homes decarbonised in 2026.

articles.jina_text:
The world has again convened for Cop, the annual ritual to confront humanity’s greatest-ever threat. Aside from its own lore and acronyms, this conference is starting to feel a little like Groundhog Day.
Representatives from almost all countries, bar the recalcitrant version of the US under Donald Trump, are here in Antalya, Turkey, to face a familiar if worsening challenge. (Even the Taliban are attending.)

The UN, which oversees these talks, has acknowledged the obvious fact that the previously agreed 1.5C global temperature-rise limit is set to be breached in just a few years, with the Earth amassing heat at an accelerating pace.
Wealthy countries, though, are still failing to meet commitments to assist poorer, vulnerable nations to cope with climate impacts. We are still cutting emissions far too slowly. We are still bickering over who should shoulder the most responsibility for this.


So what’s to be gained from Cop31? We’ll go into what to expect over the next two weeks, after this week’s most important reads – and a reminder that, through Cop31, Down to Earth will be coming to you twice a week from Guardian reporters here in Antalya.
Essential reads
 
 
Cop31: what is at stake at the UN climate summit and what can it achieve?  
 
‘A new age of climate extremes’: Earth accumulating heat at accelerating rate  
 
Alien menace or victim of xenophobia? The battle over Britain’s parakeets  
In focus


View image in fullscreen
This year’s summit is an ‘implementation’ Cop. Photograph: Antonio Bat/EPA


Since 1995, Cops have been vital in bringing the world together on the vexed question of the climate crisis, using the unwieldy cudgel of consensus decision-making and peer pressure to help forge the Paris agreement to limit the damage.
In many respects, this has been a success – at one point, the planet was staring down the barrel of a cataclysmic 4C temperature rise this century. That increase is now more in the range of 2.5C, aided by booming growth in clean energy. Such a warping of our climate is still disastrous (just think of the hellish summer many endured merely with the current level of global heating), but Cop has helped steer us away from even worse.
Still, some of the 100,000 delegates gathering here on the Mediterranean coast have been asking what, exactly, can be done here? The terms of the challenge don’t need further debate or agreement, we just have to start following through on our collective promise. Cop31 is another “implementation” Cop – its success hinges on countries going home afterwards and actually implementing things, rather than making more promises in an air-conditioned conference hall.
Political realities in other areas intrude like never before, too: the world is largely focused on war, inflation and a fracturing geopolitical order instead of the climate crisis. “This year’s fossil fuel cost chaos has delivered a global shock wave, hitting households hard and spreading inflation like a cancer,” Simon Stiell, the UN

US and rest of world must follow China’s lead on green energy, says John Kerry


Former US secretary of state says most nations are ‘stumbling along’ while Beijing has ‘hugely accelerated’ 
 
 
Cop31 live – latest updates  




China is leading the world in moving away from fossil fuels, and the rest of the globe – including the US – must now follow, the former US secretary of state John Kerry has told the Guardian, as Cop watchers wonder exactly how China is going to approach this year’s climate summit.
As Cop31 opens – this year the climate conference is in Turkey – there is plenty of speculation about whether China will finally step into the leadership role that it has long avoided. In its latest “five-year plan” adopted in March 2026, China for the first time pledged to “actively participate in and lead global climate governance”. Cop31 could provide the first indications Beijing is ready to put that rhetoric into action, something it has historically been reluctant to do.

Green energy is a vital component of the export engine that has kept China’s sluggish post-pandemic economy on track. The success of its exports stands in contrast to its failure to significantly boost domestic general consumption, a structural weakness that has persistently vexed leaders.
In 2025, clean-tech exports surpassed $220bn, and they should grow again this year; the world’s largest emitter is now the world’s leading supplier of clean energy technology. China accounts for about 85% of solar and 80% of lithium-ion battery supply chain production capacity, and in 2025, nearly 75% of electric cars were manufactured there.


View image in fullscreen
Electric cars imported from China at Southampton docks, UK. Photograph: Filby Photography/Alamy
Smart moves now by China would position it as a linchpin in a future electrostate world order, persuade rivals to cooperate, and solidify its influence in the global south.


Meanwhile other countries, including the US under Donald Trump, have fallen badly behind. Kerry said they would lose out economically – as well as putting the climate in further danger – unless they, too, embraced low-carbon power and rapid electrification. “The only country that has hugely accelerated is China. The rest of the world is stumbling along while Mother Nature is sending us more powerful signals every week, every day,” he said.

articles.jina_text:
Soaring oil and gas prices following the war in Iran have encouraged people to look beyond fossil fuels, leading to an easing of climate-damaging carbon emissions this year.
Carbon dioxide from oil, gas and coal is forecast to flatline for 2026, based on data from the year so far, according to a comprehensive assessment by scientists. Emissions from burning oil alone will drop by 2% as drivers economise on fuel use and flock to electric vehicles instead.



View image in fullscreen
Electric vehicles charge in the parking lot of the Ultium Cells facility in Lordstown, Ohio, in the US Photograph: Quinn Glabicki/Reuters
The findings, presented on Tuesday morning at the Cop31 climate talks hosted by Turkey in Antalya, show both the impact of the Iran war and the global expansion of cheap renewable energy, chiefly solar and wind power.
Talk of a global turnaround would be premature, however, the report’s authors and other analysts said. The report was published in Nature Climate Change. The reduction in emissions from fossil fuels for 2026 will be about 0.4% compared with last year.

Yet this year’s slight fall could be temporary, and was more than offset by increased emissions from deforestation and land use change, following major fires in south-east Asia and further conversions of wild land to agriculture.


Many factors could disrupt the fragile trend of slowing emissions from fossil fuels, including an intensified expansion of coal in India, an easing of oil prices and US president Donald Trump’s enthusiasm for fossil fuels. Much greater investment in renewable energy, and low-carbon technology such as electric vehicles, would still be required to make permanent reductions in annual emissions, the report’s authors said.
Glen Peters, research professor at the Cicero Centre for International Climate Research, said: “A drop in emissions in one year is not a peak, unless it is driven by structural change. Accelerated deployment of solar, wind, batteries and electric vehicles are pushing emissions down in dozens of countries, and slowing emissions growth in many more, but the changes are not sufficient to lock in a peak in global emissions.”
About 38.2bn tonnes of CO2 will be emitted this year, according to the Global Carbon Budget, an annual assessment by scientists from scores of universities and science institutions around the world, published in the journal Earth System Science Data.



Energy demand continues to increase around the world, as more people gain access to electricity and are pulled out of poverty, but two-thirds of the increase is being met from rising generation from the sun and wind and the uptake of electric vehicles.
On the downside, emissions from deforestation and the conversion of land to agriculture have also ticked upward this year, leading to total carbon emissions rising slightly for the year, from 42.8bn tonnes last year to 43.3bn forecast for 2026.

Dense fog has led to a “high” air pollution alert being issued in London, as forecasters warn of transport delays and difficult travel conditions across much of the country.




Government monitoring recorded the South East and East Midlands as having “high” pollution, with Greater London recorded as “very high”.








The Met Office earlier issued a yellow fog warning for parts of England and Wales, with visibility reduced to less than 100m in some places overnight.




Dense fog has led to a “high” air pollution alert being issued in London, as forecasters warn of difficult travel conditions across much of the country




Forecasters at Imperial College London advised Lord Sadiq Khan of Tooting to trigger the alert “after dense fog and very light winds allowed pollution to build up over the weekend, and linger into Monday morning”, according to the mayor’s office.




It said that smoke from Bonfire Night and Diwali fireworks “is likely to have contributed”.




Londoners have been advised to walk, cycle and use public transport more frequently, drive less and avoid unnecessary burning at home.




Mete Coban, the deputy mayor for environment and energy, said: “Toxic air is responsible for thousands of premature deaths in London each year, which is why the mayor has done everything in his power to tackle it, which includes launching the world’s largest clean air zone.




“It is really important we all do our bit to protect those who are most vulnerable as we continue working to build a safer and greener London for all.”




The alert is the fourth issued in the capital this year, with the last one made in June during a heatwave.












A yellow fog warning is in place until 10am on Tuesday, with the Met Office forecasting a “night of dense fog”.




The affected area stretches from Luton to Manchester, covering parts of central and northern England and Wales.








The Met Office has said slower journey times with delays to public transport are possible, with a chance of delays or cancellation of flights.




The fog is expected to develop across the warning area on Monday evening and will become dense at times overnight – with visibility reduced to less than 100m, according to the forecaster.




It will thin and clear during Tuesday morning, but will give way to cooler and frosty weather later in the week.

articles.jina_text:
Good morning. After another year of unprecedented droughts, floods and wildfires driven by human-caused global heating, 91 heads of government will meet tomorrow in Turkey to discuss the climate crisis. They will do so against a backdrop of global instability and conflict.
But as high-ranking officials and civil society campaigners settle in for a fortnight of speeches, protests and labyrinthine negotiations at the UN’s 31st annual climate conference, Cop31, many are asking what the point is.

Those same governments pledged more than a decade ago in Paris, at Cop21, to limit global heating to 1.5C above preindustrial levels, but implementation has been sclerotic, and only two months ago a UN report warned temperatures will reach at least 1.8C using even the most optimistic future projections.
I spoke to the Guardian’s environment editor Fiona Harvey in Turkey about what’s on the Cop31 agenda, what success looks like and why Brazil’s re-elected president Lula will be the star of the conference.
Five big stories
 
 
UK | Russell Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on Monday after a judge praised his victims’ bravery and accused him of living “unhindered by the rules by which decent people live”.  
 
US | Donald Trump, Elon Musk and prominent finance moguls have expressed their support for embattled Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, as the head of the world’s most valuable chip company faces an internal investigation over a romantic relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.  
 
Russia | US officials said they would seek a “final end” to the war between Russia and Ukraine, beginning with trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday in the first substantive negotiations between the two countries since February.  
 
Technology | Palantir lobbied a health minister to consider extending its AI technology into GP records, stretching its reach into the NHS in a way doctors fear could undermine trust with patients.  
 
Climate | Soaring oil and gas prices following the war in Iran have encouraged people to look beyond fossil fuels, leading to an easing of climate-damaging carbon emissions this year.  
In depth: Why the world is still failing to turn climate promises into action

articles.title: The swan sanctuary wetland fighting climate change
articles.raw_rss: The global campaign to restore the "soggy secret weapon" that can combat against climate change.
articles.raw_meta: The global campaign to restore the "soggy secret weapon" that can combat against climate change.
articles.jina_text:
Most people know rainforests are vital in the fight against climate change, but now scientists say wetlands could be even more important.
Saltmarshes, mangrove swamps and wetlands can absorb carbon "four times faster than trees", according to the charity the Wildfowl and Wetlands Trust (WWT).
Celebrating 80 years since WWT's first wetland bird reserve was founded at Slimbridge, in Gloucestershire, the charity's leaders have called for one million hectares of wetlands to be restored across the world.
Sarah Fowler, CEO of WWT, said: "They are mood-boosting, flood-buffering, water-purifying, incredible habitats. But we have lost 85% of the world's wetlands."





Image caption, 

Sir Peter Scott feeds migrating swans and geese at Slimbridge in 1947, with Desmond Hawkins, BBC features producer from Bristol




WWT now runs 10 wetland bird reserves across the UK.
Many people come to enjoy the swans, geese, flamingoes and migrating wildfowl, but do not realise how powerful these habitats can be in soaking up carbon and slowing down climate change.
So how vital are wetlands for birds, and how powerful can they be in the fight against climate change?



'Patron Saint of Conservation'




In November 1946, a naturalist called Peter Scott came to a wild marshy area on the banks of the River Severn, near Slimbridge. He was drawn by the thousands of migrating geese and swans that flew thousands of miles from the Russian Arctic to spend the winter here on the mudflats and marshes.
Captivated, Scott settled in a small cottage and later built a house right on a lake, with a huge window to watch the wildfowl. 
He dug lakes and connecting channels, built hides and even towers to watch the birds without disturbing them.
Over the years, the reserve grew and became home to thousands of ducks, swans , geese as well as the migrating wildfowl.




Image source, WWT Slimbridge
Image caption, 

Sir Peter Scott with the first nine Nēnē geese he hand-reared at Slimbridge in 1952




"He really was a pioneer in conservation," said Chris Moore, a historian of Slimbridge and author of Peter Scott and the Birth of Modern Conservation.
As well as creating a safe haven for endangered species, Scott was a vigorous campaigner for nature. 
He led the fight to stop commercial whaling, presented some of the BBC's first natural history programmes called live from Slimbridge, and helped set up WWF, the World Wildlife Fund.
In 1973 Sir Peter Scott became the first person to be knighted for conservation work.
Moore explained: "Scott was talking about the impact that man was having on the natural world, long before we started talking about climate change and global warming.
"David Attenborough called him the Patron Saint of Conservation, and I think that is more than deserved," Moore added.

Left: Solar panels in Spotsylvania county, Virginia, on 9 July. Right: Emissions billow out of the stacks at a coal-fired power plant in Pennsylvania in December 2017. Composite: EPA, Bloomberg via Getty Images


Senate advances bill to speed up projects from gas pipelines to clean energy


Key environmental groups come out against bipartisan Baaja bill over fears it could spur datacenters and ICE jails




The Senate on Monday advanced bipartisan legislation aimed at speeding up permitting reviews for datacenters and other infrastructure projects, in the first major action since last week’s election that soundly repudiated Donald Trump and congressional Republicans.
It’s a bill that would make it easier to build big infrastructure projects in America – everything from fossil fuel pipelines to transmission lines that would add more clean energy to the grid. And it would roll back environmental and social protections to achieve this goal. That is why climate advocates are torn over the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs act (Baaja).

The Senate voted on Monday to open debate on Baaja in the first of several procedural votes. Senators voted 73-25 on the cloture motion, which did not result in the bill being passed, but pushed it another step forward.



Trump urged all senators to vote for the 417-page bill, which is sponsored by two Republicans and two Democrats in the Senate, but after last week’s historic “blue wave” elections, some environmental and tribal advocates called on Democratic leadership to pump the brakes.
Earthjustice, the Sierra Club and the ACLU have come out against the bill because it would significantly weaken environmental laws including the National Environmental Policy Act (Nepa) and accelerate the construction of gas pipelines and ICE detention centers.
Indigenous groups held a press conference on Friday calling on senators to vote against Baaja because it would weaken the federal government’s legal obligation to consult tribes on projects that affect them.
“This is such an existential threat to Indian country,” said Mark Macarro, president of the National Congress of American Indians.

For two years, Americans have witnessed a largely unchecked assault on the foundations of US democracy. Authoritarian leadership has enriched itself through corruption, spread lies and launched relentless attacks on press freedom, voting rights, due process and many fundamental civil rights.
Last night, America’s embattled embattled democracy came roaring back to life: from Texas to Ohio to South Carolina, Americans surged to the polls to fight for a different path forward. The process worked, the people spoke, the candidates – and the president – accepted the results. Today, we’re on the cusp of a new chapter for America, where the people have claimed their right to hold power to account, and millions are looking at politics with a new and unfamiliar feeling of hope. 
The past two years have delivered a chilling lesson in just how fragile our fundamental freedoms are, when precious few powerful institutions are willing to stand up for the truth and defend our basic rights and freedoms. Major law firms and universities capitulated to a bullying president’s threats and intimidation. Some corporate news outlets bowed to his pressure, too.
In the face of these attacks, the independent press stood out as one of the only forces for accountability, dedicated to uncovering the truth – and making sure the public understood what was at stake in this election.
At its best, a truly free press can speak directly to the public, shedding light on hidden schemes and revealing the whole picture of our flawed world. Yet these are challenging times for press freedom: Trump’s crackdown on the press shows no signs of letting up; consolidated ownership means fewer options and less diversity of perspective; and the advent of AI has threatened the entire business model of journalism, resulting in extreme staff layoffs that have gutted newsrooms.

Chris Bowen faces a titanic task at Cop31. What will it take for the world to make the climate crisis its top priority?

Adam Morton



Whether the global community can bring itself to name fossil fuels as the cause of the climate emergency will be at the centre of debate in Antalya




Australian politics could have looked markedly different this week if the Albanese government had succeeded in its longstanding bid to host a major UN climate summit in Adelaide.
Tens of thousands of people, including ministers and diplomats representing 200 countries, would have descended on the city of the toxic algal bloom to meet, lobby and negotiate over how to tackle the climate crisis, and wander the halls of a massive green trade fair that runs alongside the formal talks.

For two weeks, it would have been the biggest news story in the country. It would have blocked out the sun. Instead, an estimated 100,000 people are flooding the streets of Antalya, a Turkish resort city on the Mediterranean, for the summit known as Cop31.







High fossil fuel prices spread inflation ‘like a cancer’, UN climate chief tells Cop31

Read more
Some senior members of the Albanese cabinet are not sorry they are so far away and lost enthusiasm for hosting the event before the final decision was made. Aside from the climate change and energy minister, Chris Bowen, the government has shown a diminishing appetite to make the case that fighting global heating is a top priority.
It still has the policies it brought in after the 2022 election – to underwrite large-scale renewable energy, make electric vehicles more available and affordable, and put a limit on industrial pollution – and last year added a generous household battery subsidy scheme. But meeting its emissions reduction targets will require significantly more. So far, those steps are MIA.
Meanwhile, the government continues to approve new coal and gas extraction, mostly for export. Since its election, 38 developments have been given the green light.
It continued a long-term trend. Since 2005 – the year against which Australia measures its emissions reduction targets – annual domestic emissions are estimated to have fallen by 25%. But, according to analysis by Naru Research, emissions from burning Australian fossil fuels after they are exported overseas have roughly doubled. articles.title: Taxpayer-funded bodies accused of costing Britain billions and blocking major projects
articles.raw_rss:
Unelected bodies are costing taxpayers hundreds of millions of pounds and delaying major infrastructure projects for years, a think tank said, as it calls for a sweeping "bonfire of the quangos".A damning new report, backed by Conservative deputy leader Alex Burghart, calls for a clear-out of taxpayer-funded bodies accused of wielding too much power with too little accountability.It highlights a £100million tunnel built to protect bats from HS2 trains and a £700million scheme to stop fish being sucked into a nuclear power station as examples of environmental requirements sending costs soaring.And it reveals that more than 300 public bodies employed around 397,000 people in 2023-24 - two-thirds more than a decade earlier.

A worker at the Zubair oil and gas field in Iraq. Scientists have confirmed global heating will reach at least 1.8C, beyond the 1.5C goal set at talks in 2015. Photograph: Haidar Mohammed Ali/AFP/Getty


High fossil fuel prices spread inflation ‘like a cancer’, UN climate chief tells Cop31


Simon Stiell makes opening address at summit in Turkey, where talks are under way about speeding up shift to electrification




A global fossil fuel price crisis is “spreading inflation like a cancer” around the planet, the UN’s climate chief, Simon Stiell, told the opening plenary of critical UN climate talks in Turkey.
Stiell joined Cop31 hosts Turkey and Australia, which is leading the negotiations, in promoting renewable energy and a new electrification goal as an optimistic alternative to a planet still tied to oil, coal and gas.

Inside the tight security of the opening plenary on Monday, delegates from almost 200 countries watched a stirring short film with scenes of fire, flood and storms that proclaimed: “It’s time to reconnect with the planet we have grown apart from.”
Turkey said it expected 100,000 visitors, including national delegations, to attend the two-week talks, including at least 95 heads of state. A global leaders summit is scheduled for Wednesday and Thursday. But the talks are under increased pressure to deliver, after growing dissatisfaction with the snail’s pace of results.


View image in fullscreen
Activists take part in a fossil of the day demonstration on the opening day of the UN Climate Change Conference in Antalya on Monday. Photograph: Murad Sezer/Reuters
The talks are opening as a historic El Niño builds in the tropical Pacific and months after a glacier collapse set off catastrophic flooding in Nepal and Tibet, wiping away villages and killing at least 1,459 people, with thousands more still missing. Climate scientists confirmed this year that global heating would reach at least 1.8C – beyond the 1.5C temperature goal that countries promised to aim for at talks in Paris in 2015.


Last week Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, told the Guardian that although he still had faith in the negotiating process, “the fact that global warming is accelerating, that we inevitably will be breaching the 1.5C limit within three to five years, that tipping points are coming closer fast … and that this is allowed to happen within the framework of the Paris agreement, cannot be considered as anything but a global failure.”
And in a statement the UN secretary general, António Guterres, urged leaders to “get serious by cutting emissions faster, accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need”.

Full SummaryThe Cop31 climate conference has opened in Antalya, Turkey, with an estimated 100,000 attendees facing logistical challenges despite a sense of optimism. UN climate change executive secretary Simon Stiell emphasized the urgency of transitioning to renewable energy and addressed the climate crisis as a global health emergency.
An estimated 100,000 people have descended on the Turkish city of Antalya for the UN’s flagship climate conference, Cop31, and everybody seems to have a story of a taxi not knowing where the official drop-off location is, a broken down shuttle bus, or a seemingly endless queue in the fierce Mediterranean sun. 
Developing country delegations have reported immense frustration at members being unable to attend opening meetings – and it took this reporter just shy of seven hours from leaving his hotel to finally arrive in the “blue” UN negotiating zone this afternoon.
Regardless of this somewhat shaky start, the message has been clear. In his opening address, UN climate change executive secretary Simon Stiell did not mince his words in highlighting how extreme climate events are hitting communities worldwide – while also calling for an urgent push for renewable solutions that are now typically much cheaper than fossil fuels. 





“Global heating is already costing the Earth: Appalling tragedy has hit the Himalayas, adding to the ever-expanding catalogue hitting communities across every region,” he said. “But the solutions are clear: Global renewables saved around half a trillion dollars last year. And another $265 billion in the first half of this year alone.” 
"The urgency of this moment must drive us forward," Stiell added.

articles.jina_text:
The energy secretary has stressed that affordability is her "overriding objective", as she said reducing bills would be key to maintaining public support for climate action.
Speaking to BBC Panorama, Miatta Fahnbulleh insisted that the government's drive for cleaner power would help to cut energy bills in the long term.
But she conceded that the push to reduce carbon emissions was currently "under pressure" amid discontent at rising prices in recent years.
It comes as ministers grapple with how to respond to a predicted surge in energy prices in January, expected to mark the biggest rise in bills for four years.







Scientists predict 2026 hottest year on record as climate talks begin





Government's EV targets expected to be reduced this week
Labour has faced extra political pressure over its climate ambitions since coming to power, as Reform UK rose in opinion polls and the Conservatives under Kemi Badenoch disowned their previous ambition of reaching net zero by 2050.
Both opposition parties have taken particular aim at public subsidy schemes designed to boost renewable sources of electricity generation, arguing that the drive for cleaner energy has driven up costs for consumers.
UK households currently pay one of the highest rates for electricity in Europe. 














Bills have increased due to subsidies but also because of the high price of gas (a fossil fuel) driven up by international conflicts.

Three reasons why UK electricity prices are so high
Asked during her Panorama interview what her main task was, Fahnbulleh replied: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt."
In the interview, which was recorded last week, and aired on Monday night, she argued that Labour's push for greener electricity was "one of our routes to delivering affordability".
"The drive to clean power is about decoupling our dependence on global fossil fuel markets," she added. "Ultimately if we have homegrown renewables, nuclear, that's the way in which we will drive bills in the long term."
However, she conceded that struggles over energy affordability were part of the reason the consensus on climate action was "under pressure".
"People want to blame net zero for that. Now, I don't believe that's the case.
"But I'm very clear that part of the way in which we build and maintain public consent is that we've got to show that this transition, which we have to do on climate grounds, is good for people's pockets."





The UK had a record number of heatwaves this summer and suffered successive damaging wildfires, which the Met Office has said was made 130 times more likely by climate change.
Just last month, whilst hosting the UK's first summit on wildfires, Andy Burnham acknowledged that as a result of climate change "the summer we've just had is likely to be a more regular situation going forward".
But he has also vowed to lead a "cost of living government" and reindustralise the economy.

The 31st UN climate summit opened in Antalya, Turkey, co-hosted by Australia, which is leading the formal negotiations.  
 
An agenda was quickly agreed – avoiding a fight that has cropped up in previous years – but tensions over money have already begun to rise.  
 
The World Meteorological Organisation warned that the Earth is heating at an accelerating rate, supercharging weather extremes.

The EU is almost on track to meet its 2030 climate targets, an official report has found, but efforts to cut pollution fall well short of its 2040 and 2050 targets.
The report, published today by the European Environment Agency (EEA), found EU emissions fell by 1.6% in 2025, though at a slower pace than the year before and not deeply enough to put it on track to meet its goals. If all planned climate policies are put in place, its net emissions should fall by 54% from 1990 levels by the end of the decade, just shy of its legally binding target of 55%.
Europe is among the biggest historical polluters of planet-heating gas, having begun the Industrial Revolution and exported its economic system around the world. In recent decades, though, it has championed some of the most dramatic reductions in pollution. The average European now pollutes a little less carbon than the average Chinese person. Both regions have per-capita emissions well below that of the US, Canada and Australia, though considerably greater than India, Brazil and Indonesia.
The EEA report found EU emission reductions in the next five years must be as high as those achieved over the last two decades to meet its targets. Full SummaryUnder the EU's Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive, businesses selling to EU shoppers are prohibited from using terms like 'carbon neutral' or 'climate neutral' if those claims rely on offsets purchased outside a product's direct supply chain. The directive aims to eliminate vague environmental marketing by requiring specific proof and independent certification for green claims.
Few people get to watch their own word being pushed out of use in real time. Fewer still celebrate. "I regret coining the phrase 'carbon neutral'," says Dan Morrell, "so I'm absolutely delighted that my word has been banned, which is an extraordinary feeling. I ended up with it in the Oxford English Dictionary and now to see it finally pass away is fantastic."
Since the end of September, under the EU's Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive, businesses selling to EU shoppers can no longer call a product "carbon neutral", "climate neutral" or "climate compensated" because they have bought offsets outside of the supply chain needed for the product itself. Vague words like "eco-friendly" and "green" are on borrowed time too. For a fashion industry fond of a leafy logo, it is the biggest shake-up of green marketing in years.

After a summer of record-breaking heatwaves, wildfires and school closures, Britain is now facing worsening drought.
Yet as the climate crisis intensifies, the international response is under mounting pressure. Countries have been accused of failing to deliver on promises made at previous UN summits, while several major powers are increasingly turning their backs on the process.
However, energy secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh has told The Independent that Britain’s participation at Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, this week is “in the national interest” – both to protect the country from increasingly extreme weather and to seize opportunities in the green economy.




“This summer, we all felt it. Record heatwaves. Homes lost to wildfires. Schools forced to close in the heat,” she said. “Climate change is no longer a warning about the future, or something happening somewhere else. It is here, in Britain, now.”
Her comments come amid growing questions over whether Cop is delivering on its promises. Donald Trump has pulled the US out of the Paris Agreement and begun the process of withdrawing from the UN climate convention, and several other world leaders are also staying away from this year’s summit.

But with the potential return of El Niño threatening to push global temperatures even higher, the prospect of further extreme weather adds urgency to the negotiations.


Key focuses for the UK at the conference, Ms Fahnbulleh suggested, will include pushing clean power, cutting methane emissions, and protecting forests and oceans. “[We will] build resilience to the extreme weather to come, and unlock the finance to make it happen,” she said. 
Ms Fahnbulleh is leading the UK delegation in Turkey, and is set to attend alongside visits from PM Andy Burnham, foreign secretary Ed Miliband, mayor of London Sadiq Khan, and net zero minister Katie White.

Miatta Fahnbulleh, the secretary of state for energy and climate change (PA)

Meanwhile, the US is not expected to send any official delegation at all, with Donald Trump having pulled out of the Paris Agreement and the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change when he returned to the White House last year.

Full SummaryThe World Meteorological Organization warns that 2026 is on track to be one of the hottest years on record as human-caused global warming interacts with a 'supersized' El Niño. Global average surface temperatures for January through September 2026 reached approximately 1.47C above pre-industrial levels, with experts predicting the 1.5C threshold set by the Paris Agreement may be exceeded by the end of the year.
2026 is on track to be one of the hottest year on record, as decades of human-caused global warming clashes with a “supersized” El Niño.
A report published by the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) on Monday warns that the last 12 years have individually been the warmest on record, with the past four years being the top four. 
The global average surface temperature for January-September 2026 was about 1.47 C above the pre-industrial average. 





But experts say this figure is likely to rise through the end of the year due to the warming effect of the naturally occurring weather phenomenon. 
The EU's Copernicus climate service already said 2026 was all but certain to become the second calendar year after 2024 to ‌exceed the threshold of 1.5C above pre-industrial ​levels set in the 2015 Paris Agreement.

articles.title: Scientists predict 2026 hottest year on record as climate talks begin

articles.jina_text:
From Western Europe to Indonesia, countries have battled wildfires throughout 2026 following record heat from climate change and El Niño





The world is on course for its hottest year on record as the planet is hit with warming from climate change and El Niño, scientists have told BBC News.
The warning comes as world leaders and negotiators gather in Turkey on Monday for the opening of COP31, the latest UN climate summit.
Berkeley Earth, the independent US research group behind the forecast, said that even with two months of the year left it is 95% confident that 2026 will surpass the previous record set in 2024.
The impact of rising heat has been felt acutely in recent months by countries attending COP, with extensive wildfires across Europe and the sudden glacier collapse in Nepal which killed more than 1,000 people.
"We have had a run of record warm years," said Dr Robert Rohde, of Berkeley Earth. "That is what we expect as global warming progresses… glaciers collapsing, record-breaking heatwaves and droughts."
On Friday, the EU's Copernicus climate service confirmed that October was the hottest on record.
But Rohde warned this was just the start. "There is potential for much larger and much more dramatic changes down the line," he said.
The main driver of rising global temperatures has been the increasing concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, largely caused by burning fossil fuels.














The UN's World Meteorological Organization (WMO) published its own report on Monday, and although more cautious than Berkeley, it has forecast that 2026 will be among the four warmest years on record.
It said that 2027 will provide no let-up, as an unusually powerful El Niño will continue into next year, pushing temperatures higher.
WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said it "gives new meaning to the phrase off the charts".


The findings underline the challenge facing negotiators gathering in the seaside Turkish city of Antalya for COP31.
At previous meetings the focus has been on reducing emissions - tackling the cause of climate change. But now an increasing number of nations are facing the reality of having to do that alongside adapting to new weather extremes as the planet warms.
"No single COP is a silver bullet. No single conference can bridge the chasm between the science and reality," Simon Stiell, the UN's climate chief, said as he addressed delegates on the opening morning.
But he added "the urgency of this moment must drive us forward. Global heating is already costing the Earth."










Last month the UK defence secretary warned the public and businesses to think about how they would cope with increasing natural disasters, including stockpiling food.

‘A new age of climate extremes’: Earth accumulating heat at accelerating rate



Increased heat will supercharge extreme weather events, warns UN agency as Cop31 climate summit begins




Heat is accumulating in Earth’s systems at an accelerating rate, the UN’s weather agency has reported as the Cop31 climate change summit begins in Turkey, with 2026 on track to be one of the four warmest years on record.
The imbalance between incoming energy from the sun and energy leaving Earth reached its highest level since monitoring began, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in its State of the Global Climate update.

That imbalance and the accumulation of heat will supercharge extreme weather events such as heatwaves, droughts and tropical cyclones.
Around the world, the average surface temperature for January to September 2026 was about 1.47C above the preindustrial average, the agency said. Sea surface temperatures hit monthly records and sea level was the highest since records began. The ocean absorbs 90% of the excess heat trapped by greenhouse gases and 2026 is on track to be a 10th successive year of record ocean heat.


View image in fullscreen
A centre for people experiencing respiratory difficulties in Palangkaraya, Indonesia. More than 11,000 people have been treated during a months-long wildfire crisis. Photograph: REINA/AFP/Getty Images
“We have entered a new age of climate extremes,” said António Guterres, the UN secretary general. “A supersized El Niño is colliding with a planet already superheated by manmade climate change. Climate records keep falling. The human costs keep rising. And those least responsible are suffering first and worst.”


Diplomats and world leaders are meeting on Monday in the Turkish resort city of Antalya for the 31st conference of the parties (Cop) to the UN framework convention on climate change. In 1992, when the convention was signed, the atmospheric concentration of carbon dioxide, the primary greenhouse gas, was 356.42 parts per million (ppm). In 2025 it was 426.8 ppm, the WMO said. Overall, since 1750, the onset of the Industrial Revolution, the concentration has increased 53%.







Cop31 must deliver climate progress that people can see is real, host says 

Read more
The WMO reported that ocean heat content estimates indicate Earth’s energy imbalance rose at a rate of 0.3W per sq metre each decade for the period 2001–2025, compared with 0.13W per sq metre between 1960 and 2025.
Accordingly, 2026 is on track to be one of the four warmest years on record globally, making 2023 to 2026 the four warmest years since records began.

Full SummaryThe Cop31 climate summit opens in Antalya, Turkey, as experts warn that global temperatures are likely to exceed the 1.5C warming limit established by the 2015 Paris Agreement. While nations gather to discuss mitigation and adaptation, activists and small island states express concern that the window to prevent an overshoot is closing due to decades of climate inaction.
The United Nations’ annual climate talks open in Turkey on Monday as Cop31 – with experts suggesting we are already heading for a long-term breach of the crucial limit of global temperatures hitting 1.5C above pre-industrial levels.
As nearly 200 countries gather for the two-week summit in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya, governments must deal with an energy crisis fuelled by the war in the Middle East and a growing list of disasters, including deadly floods in Nepal, heatwaves in Europe and wildfires in Indonesia.
These UN talks come at a time when global temperatures already stand at about 1.4C above pre-industrial levels, and 1.5C, the goal set under the 2015 Paris Agreement, is very likely to be breached. The UN Environment Programme’s latest report said last month that it is now about managing the overshoot, to then return below 1.5C.





Overshoot describes a period in which temperatures rise above 1.5C before any return below it. articles.jina_text:
The US will be absent from key UN climate talks that start on Monday, a further sign of Donald Trump’s scornful dismissal of the climate crisis. But Democrats’ crushing win in the US midterm elections has delivered a timely shot of optimism to countries now looking beyond the Trump era of climate obstruction.
For the second year in a row, there will be no official US government presence at the annual climate summit, this year known as Cop31 and held in Antalya, Turkey. While almost every other country in the world sends delegations to the talks, Trump has derided the climate crisis as a “hoax” and “bullshit” and triggered the withdrawal of the US from the entire international climate framework.

“This summit rejects reality by failing to acknowledge that extremist climate policies are destroying countries around the world,” a White House official said, confirming that the administration would not send anyone to Cop31.
The snub is so severe that about 20 members of the US Congress heading to the summit have been denied usual state department assistance, requiring them to turn to philanthropic funding for the trip. “I’m glad we found a way to get there, but it is insane,” said Sean Casten, a Democratic congressman who is attending Cop31. “We have a lot of rebuilding to do. It hinges on Congress to maintain diplomatic continuities at Cop and minimize the damage until adults are back in the White House.”


View image in fullscreen
Sean Casten, a US representative of Illinois, in New York City on 24 September 2025. Photograph: John Lamparski/Getty Images for Concordia Annual Summit
Trump’s active support of fossil fuels, evisceration of pollution limits and throttling of clean energy projects has caused the US to become an outlier among wealthy countries, a recent UN report found. While all the other 20 major economies reduced or slowed their carbon pollution last year, the US was a “major exception” by emitting an extra 133m tons of planet-heating gases from the burning of coal, oil and gas, the report states.


Despite the world rapidly surging past “safe” temperature thresholds because of such pollution, and escalating heatwaves, floods, droughts and other calamities, Trump has remained defiant. “If you don’t get away from this green scam, your country is going to fail,” the US president told other world leaders at the UN last year, adding that the climate crisis was “the greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world”.
But the Democrats’ stunning success in the midterms last week, wresting control from Trump’s Republicans in both the House of Representatives and the Senate, has buoyed delegates gathering in Antalya. While this will be the last Cop with the US as an official party, after Trump exited the UN framework, the midterms have raised international confidence of a looming return and new, post-Trump chapter.


View image in fullscreen
Flooded homes in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, on 2 November. Photograph: Cheney Orr/Colorado Sun/Zuma Press Wir

articles.jina_text:
A beef industry-funded effort to teach teenagers about cattle’s climate impact was quietly scrapped following backlash from some ranchers, who disputed the premise that cows contribute to global heating.
The episode is the latest example of the livestock industry’s decades-long battle to determine what US children learn about cows and the climate.

The American Farm Bureau Foundation for Agriculture (AFBFA) and its Food and Agriculture Center for Science Education produce a free science curriculum used by around 1.2m students across more than 100 school districts nationwide.
Late last year, the foundation announced a new lesson exploring “how cattle produce methane and its role within the broader environmental and biological systems”.







Cryosphere faces permanent damage when world overshoots 1.5C, scientists warn

Read more
Within months it had been removed, following online criticism from ranchers, with Brett Kenzy, prominent South Dakota farmer, telling a trade paper “it’s not fair claiming that cows are harming the environment because they’re not”. Kenzy, who chairs a committee of the Ranchers-Cattlemen Action Legal Fund United Stockgrowers of America (R-CALF USA), called the lesson a “slap in the face”.
“We did take it down,” Rick Henningfeld, the AFBFA education director, told an audience at CattleCon, the beef industry’s annual convention, in February. “We heard the feedback, and we are editing it, and our hope is to get it back up quickly,” according to a recording of the event shared with the Guardian.
It hasn’t yet returned. A new lesson on cattle digestion, published in July, makes no mention of methane or climate.
Since the 1990s, the beef industry has worked to shape what children learn about its products. Today, officials behind the curriculum say it “eliminate[s] negative perceptions” of the industry for “future consumers”.
The curriculum is funded by a mandatory levy on cattle sales called the “beef checkoff”. A foundation spokesperson said the topic “cannot be a 45-minute lesson”. The foundation said it is working on a longer version, reviewing research “related to the biogenic cycle” with help from unnamed researchers and university experts. It said the July lesson was “not a replacement”.
A severed climate connection
Animal agriculture advocates often claim the biogenic cycle – in which atmospheric methane breaks down within about 12 years into carbon dioxide that is then reabsorbed by grass – means cattle methane contributes little additional global heating.
But mainstream climate researchers point out that biogenic methane – which comes from living sources such as organic waste, rice paddies and livestock – is a leading cause of climate crisis, even when emissions aren’t rising.

They became legal in the UK in August and can be bought from a range of retailers including Argos, Homebase and Amazon. The Government has estimated, based on the output of a 800W solar panel kit, that the technology would save people £70 to £110 a year. 
Steel bought two 920W panels from his energy provider, Octopus Energy, at a cost of £650 including all the hardware needed for installation. 



 
The savings have been modest so far due to the weather. His best day over the past two weeks has seen him generate 3.5 kWh of electricity – worth about 90p based on his current electricity tariff.  
“It’s a bit difficult because of the season, because each day the light gets less, so it produces less,” he explained.  
But when the days get longer, Steel believes it “should subsidise for the whole of the day until it goes dark. So it should be quite a saving in the summer”. 

Steel installed the solar panels on the south-facing wall of his home 
Based on his savings so far, he has calculated it will take three to four years for the upfront cost of the panels to be paid off with savings – meaning he expects to save £160 to £215 per year.  
Rising energy bills were a crucial factor for Steel in the decision to invest.  
“Especially as a pensioner it’s something you feel you have limited control over… it’s a little bit of a safety net,” he said.

articles.raw_meta: High-stakes talks involving 190 countries begin on Monday as world grapples with El Niño supercharged by fossil fuels
articles.jina_text:
The Cop31 summit must produce progress, “a tangible outcome ... that people can see is real”, its host has said as scores of world leaders and representatives of close to 190 countries gather in Turkey for the UN climate talks.
The high-stakes meeting begins on Monday, as countries around the world grapple with the strongest El Niño weather system on record, supercharged by fossil fuels, which is set to take hundreds of thousands of lives and cause damage costing trillions of dollars.

Friction is expected between the rich and poor worlds over who pays for the impacts of the climate crisis, and the slow pace of cutting greenhouse gas emissions. Temperatures have broken records this year, surpassing the limit of 1.5C above preindustrial levels aimed for in the 2015 Paris climate agreement.
Adão Soares Barbosa, the chair of the Least Developed Countries, a negotiating group of 44 nations, said: “Keeping 1.5C within reach by minimising the duration and magnitude of the overshoot, delivering accessible and predictable climate finance, strengthening adaptation, and addressing loss and damage [caused to poor countries by extreme weather] are not political choices but matters of survival. The credibility of the Paris agreement will be measured not by promises made, but by commitments fulfilled, and lives protected in vulnerable countries.”


View image in fullscreen
Although the summit is being held in Turkey, the formal negotiations will be presided over by Australia.  Photograph: Sandro Basili/Shutterstock
Unusually, the talks will have dual hosts: they will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya but the formal negotiations will be presided over by Australia, following a compromise reached last year over their competing bids.

We need progress, it needs to be a step forward on previous Cops.”

But climate advocates and more than 500 scientists in Australia said Australia must stop approving coalmines and gas projects if it wanted to escape the charge of hypocrisy.

Trump administration has gutted regulations that protect lives and natural resources as pipeline build-out continues




Datacenters are spurring a boom in fossil fuel pipeline projects at a time when the Trump administration is gutting rules that protect from disasters along the lines, a new review of federal records shows.
The report, compiled by the Environmental Integrity Project, also found pipelines are being built to meet demand for natural gas exports fueled by wars in Ukraine and Iran. Federal records identified almost 200 pipeline projects that are proposed or in the works, and would collectively span 17,000 miles (27,000km).

Not only has the Trump administration targeted laws that protect the environment and human health from pipelines’ risks, it has also pledged not to enforce regulations around them, the report adds.







Datacenters were on the ballot. US voters rejected them

Read more
The findings bring into focus a little-considered environmental threat in artificial intelligence and datacenter proliferation – the US already records about 1.7 pipeline accidents, spills, fires or explosions per day, and these projects would almost certainly lead to more.
The pipelines could help supply the at least 98 gas-fired power plants proposed to serve datacenters, and, if all the lines are completed, they would transport about 40% more natural gas daily than what the system carries today.
“This is the largest boom in a couple decades … and it coincides with all this deregulation,” Alexandra Shaykevich, research manager with the Environmental Integrity Project, said. “That’s concerning because the pipelines do usually operate safely, but they can leak and explode, and so there are big risks for communities across the United States.”


Most of the pipelines would carry natural gas across 42 states, though many of them are concentrated in several fossil fuel-producing regions. About 42 are in or cross Texas, 27 are in Louisiana, and nine each are in Pennsylvania and Illinois.
Advocates say they’re especially worried because of the wide-ranging attacks on foundational environmental protections, from the Clean Water Act to the Endangered Species Act, that until recently have been wielded to stop the riskiest projects, protect from accidents or hold polluters accountable.

articles.jina_text:
Hosting Cop was a key pledge from Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese in 2021, while in opposition, before his successful election campaign. But arcane rules meant the country had to wait its turn to bid and was then embroiled in an angry row with Turkey over the hosting. The final compromise put Australia in charge of the negotiations which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya. The bitter taste left by the row lingers and Australia has seemed to some a rather half-hearted host. The country’s media has been much quieter on Cop than previous host countries, and although Albanese will speak at the opening of the leaders’ segment, he is unlikely to stay long.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister, will be in daily charge of the negotiations. As aspects of Australia’s energy supply also fall under his portfolio, he has been in the sometimes uncomfortable position of having to boost fossil fuels while insisting on the need for a clean energy transition.


View image in fullscreen
Chris Bowen in the House of Representatives in Canberra. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP
Yet Australia has a positive story to tell on decarbonisation: while remaining one of the world’s major fossil fuel exporters, the country has also invested heavily in renewables, and solar power has now expanded so much that consumers are sometimes offered free electricity.
Turkey


Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, Turkey’s autocratic president, showed little interest in climate and environmental concerns before bidding to host this year’s Cop summit.
In the last five years, Cop has also been held in Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, Azerbaijan, all in the same broad region. This has given an outsize role to the Arab group of countries, who are neighbours in the region and have a strong interest in ensuring that fossil fuel interests – including their lobbyists – are well represented.
Australia runs the overall direction of the negotiations, and Turkey’s government, with the environment minister, Murat Kurum, has control of the action agenda, a programme of voluntary initiatives. Erdoğan has used this to push forward a key interest of his wife, Emine Erdoğan, in cutting waste and promoting the circular economy. She has called for an end to “throwaway culture” and for recycling instead of landfill – though Turkey still has sites that leak vast quantities of methane.


View image in fullscreen
Emine Erdoğan has called for an end to ‘throwaway culture’. Photograph: Ahmet Serdar Eser/Anadolu/Getty Images
Fatih Birol, the head of the International Energy Agency and one of the world’s leading energy economists, is understood to be one of the advisers behind this year’s emphasis on electrification, displacing fossil fuels with electricity for heating, transport and industrial uses. This could halve the amount of energy we need, and is the next biggest step, after boosting renewable energy generation, needed for a low-carbon world.

An unprecedented record early polar vortex breakdown could leave Britain in a cold snap and even blanketed in snow later this month.

The unusual phenomenon, potentially prompted by the El Niño effect, may see the vortex – a large circulation of strong winds high above the Arctic Circle – weaken and even split, thereby sending colder air further south.

British winters are usually kept relatively mild and wet by a constant straight jet stream over the North Atlantic.

View image in fullscreen
Turkey is hosting Cop31 in Antalya, while Australia will lead the formal negotiations under an unusual power-sharing agreement. Photograph: Sandro Basili/Shutterstock



Explainer
Cop31: what is at stake at the UN climate summit and what can it achieve?



Delegates from more than 190 countries are gathering in Turkey for climate talks, but the US will be absent




As the planet faces unprecedented human-caused global heating, heads of government are meeting for the next fortnight for the latest round of climate talks. We ask why it matters and what is likely to be achieved.


What is Cop31?
From 9-20 November, world leaders, ministers and high-ranking officials from more than 190 countries are expected to convene in Antalya in Turkey, for the annual UN climate talks. This year, the summit will be hosted by Turkey, but in an unusual twist the negotiations will be presided over by Australia in a compromise deal struck after the two countries vied for the presidency.







Who’s who at Cop31: key players at the climate talks

Read more
While nearly all of the 196 original signatories of the 2015 Paris climate agreement are expected to be present, one glaring absence will be the US, whose president, Donald Trump, has withdrawn from Paris.

How will co-convening work?
Australia will take charge of the formal negotiations where countries thrash out the details of work programmes such as the “just transition”, climate finance and putting the world on track to stick as closely as possible to the Paris agreement goal of limiting temperature rises to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels.


View image in fullscreen
The Paris climate agreement was adopted in 2015, committing countries to pursue efforts to limit global heating to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels. Photograph: François Mori/AP


Turkey will take charge of the “action agenda”, the voluntary agreements that work towards the Paris goals but are not legally binding: programmes on cutting waste and achieving a circular economy, cutting methane, improving food security, and – perhaps most important – the electrification of the global economy.

What are likely to be the key issues?
The Paris goal of 1.5C has been breached, but the UN argues that rapid action to cut greenhouse gas emissions would limit the “overshoot” and allow for a return to lower temperatures by the end of this century. For that to happen, countries need to break dependence on fossil fuels and adopt low-carbon technologies faster. The two roadmaps from Brazil – on the “transition away from fossil fuels” and on halting deforestation – will present ways of doing so.

A survivor in a house damaged by flash floods in Nepal. Developing countries are calling for more financial support to cope with severe climate-related disas

articles.title: Countryside managers prepare for climate change
articles.raw_rss: North Pennines National Landscape's plan includes restoring peatland and wildfire preparedness.
articles.raw_meta: North Pennines National Landscape's plan includes restoring peatland and wildfire preparedness.
articles.jina_text:
Climate change readiness and helping people access the countryside are among priorities in a five-year plan for a national landscape.
The North Pennines National Landscape Management Plan 2026-31 has been adopted by the Cumberland, Westmorland and Furness, County Durham and Northumberland councils.
Work to ensure the North Pennines was "as prepared as possible for future climate challenges" included restoring peatland to help reduce flooding and equipping farmers with wildfire fighting equipment such as drones.
Chris Woodley-Stewart, director of the North Pennines National Landscape (NPNL), said: "In many ways, its the most ambitious plan that we've ever had, but also the most realistic."
National landscapes were formerly known as areas of outstanding natural beauty, and the North Pennines features heather moors, dales, woods and one of England's highest waterfalls High Force.
NPNL is mainly funded by the government and other charitable organisations.
One of the priorities in its management plan announced last month was adapting to "warmer, wetter winters and hotter, drier summers".




Image source, Getty Images
Image caption, 

The area is home to High Force waterfall




NPNL said uplands were "especially vulnerable to the effects of climate change" through rising temperatures, altered rainfall patterns, and increased frequency of extreme weather events.
Mitigation work like protecting existing woodlands and restoring carbon-rich peat soils would help safeguard upland ecosystems but also support downstream communities by "improving water quality and reducing flooding", it said.
One of the area's largest land managers, Raby Estates, said it worked with NPNL on wildfire prevention measures including managing its farmers' fuel loads and providing firefighting equipment.
Duncan Peake, chief executive at Raby Estates, said drone equipment to help spot fires was a "really significant, additional tool in our wildfire control kit".
As part of the management plan, NPNL said it was would also work with farmers who wanted to get the skills and equipment for farm visits.
Peake said farmers on their estate were already taking groups of mostly young people "who wouldn't normally have an opportunity to come to the countryside" to help them understand how farming works.
Woodley-Stewart said: "You can't make people come to the countryside and invest in the local economy, but you can help to create circumstances in which they feel this landscape is for everybody."
He said the five-year plan would guide the policy of the local authorities but would not be compulsory.
"There's no stick here, it's all carrot," Woodley-Stewart said, adding: "Everyone has a role to play in its implementation."

articles.jina_text:
Banana producers in Latin America are calling for better pay to help cope with the impact of the climate crisis, as they face big drops in production resulting from extreme weather during this year’s super El Niño event.
High winds in parts of Colombia, one of the biggest suppliers to the UK market where droughts are predicted in some regions this year, and heavy rainfall in Peru and Ecuador are already affecting production, according to the Fairtrade Foundation ethical trade body. In the Dominican Republic, farmers are expected to face drought conditions, with forecasts of drier and warmer than usual conditions.

Fairtrade research suggests that during the previous El Niño cycle, productivity across its farmers and workers dropped by 13% in the Dominican Republic, 22% in Ecuador, and 6% in Peru compared with the year before. The El Niño event in 1983 – one of the strongest ever recorded – affected 15% of total planted banana area in Ecuador, with a reduction in exports of 36%.


Dr Carley-Jane Stanton, a climate and environment lead at Fairtrade, says this El Niño is expected to lead to more extreme weather, including heavy rainfall and strong winds and “we expect the impacts for producers to be more severe” than in the 23-24 cycle.
Evidence is mounting to fuel those fears. Exports from the Colombian Caribbean region fell 32% to $122m (£91m) between July and September this year, according to the Association of Banana Growers of Magdalena and La Guajira, as reported by the trade publication Fruitnet.
It said that in September alone, shipments were down 42% year on year, with earnings close to halving to $40m from $70m.
“Given the risks threatening the continuity of banana production, we are calling on international markets to foster commercial conditions that recognise actual production costs and contribute to the sector’s sustainability,” the association said.
It said that climate-related productivity losses and a decline in earnings from exports made worse by currency issues was “undermining the economic sustainability of the industry”.
Ever Antonio Flores Muños, a worker at the Agrosiete banana producer in Colombia, told Fairtrade: “Over the past 10 years the climate has changed a lot. It’s been getting much hotter … it’s really intense. Some places have had losses due to the climate, flooding, strong winds. It’s going to affect all of us – our workers, colleagues – everything will be at great risk, and our wages will decrease.”


Fairtrade is calling for legislation in the UK to tackle unfair trading practices, such as low or late payments to farmers and contracts which push risk down the supply chain, so that producers can invest more into improving their crops’ resilience to severe weather and more likelihood of pests and diseases. Worker health is also expected to be affected by more extreme weather.
